points.t: A pustule or small wound that rapidly becomes an exquisitely painful ulcer with a violaceous, overhanging edge, often in a patient with IBD or rheumatoid arthritis.
Neutrophilic autoinflammation, not infection. Trauma makes it worse (pathergy).
Recognise it and refer urgently. Specialist treatment with oral steroids or ciclosporin. No wide debridement.
Misdiagnosis as an infected ulcer, with repeated antibiotics and surgical debridement that make it worse.

points: Inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis more than Crohn’s)
Drugs, e.g. cocaine contaminated with levamisole
**Pathergy:** minor trauma (a graze, a needle, surgery, a stoma, debridement) triggers or worsens lesions in ~25–30%. **The case: a car-door graze → pustule within days → painful ulcer.**
Starts as a pustule, papule or haemorrhagic blister, often after a **minor injury**, then becomes a deep ulcer within days.
Classic **purple, overhanging (undermined) edge** with a necrotic or purulent base.
**Severe pain**, out of proportion to the size.
Legs most often; also around stomas in IBD, and at surgical sites (pathergy).

**Sites:** **pretibial skin (commonest)**; also trunk, head and neck, **peristomal skin**, post-surgical wounds (breast surgery, caesarean section), genitals; rarely mucosa and internal organs (sterile neutrophilic abscesses in lung, spleen).

— a weighted score from German wound clinics (rapid progression, assessment of differentials, violaceous border as the main items); a total of **≥ 10 points** suggests PG. Useful as a teaching checklist.
Clinical, after **excluding** infection, vasculitis and malignancy. Biopsy of the edge supports the diagnosis (neutrophilic infiltrate; Delphi/Maverakis criteria).
Swabs only to look for secondary infection.

cards.name: Infection — S. aureus/streptococcal ecthyma, necrotising soft-tissue infection, atypical mycobacteria (M. marinum, M. chelonae, M. ulcerans), deep fungal infection, herpes simplex (immunosuppressed), leishmaniasis, synergistic gangrene
cards.clue: Responds to the right antimicrobial; tissue culture/PCR positive; atypical mycobacterial ulcers usually evolve **over weeks to months**; on azathioprine, infection must be excluded first

cards.name: Martorell (hypertensive ischaemic) ulcer
cards.clue: Older patient with **long-standing hypertension ± diabetes**; very painful necrotic ulcer on the **lateral or posterior lower leg / Achilles area**; subcutaneous arteriolosclerosis on deep biopsy. **Debridement and skin grafting help Martorell but worsen PG** — so the distinction matters

cards.name: Vasculitis and vasculopathy — GPA, PAN, cryoglobulinaemia, rheumatoid vasculitis, antiphospholipid syndrome, livedoid vasculopathy, calciphylaxis
cards.clue: Palpable purpura, livedo racemosa, nodules, renal involvement; ANCA, cryoglobulins, APL antibodies; calciphylaxis in renal failure

cards.name: Venous, arterial and neuropathic ulcers
cards.clue: Site, ABPI, varicose veins and haemosiderin, neuropathy; less painful and slower (venous/neuropathic)

cards.name: Malignancy — SCC (including Marjolin ulcer in a chronic wound), BCC, lymphoma
cards.clue: Rolled or heaped edge, slower growth, no inflammatory violaceous border; biopsy

cards.name: Other
cards.clue: Factitious ulcers (bizarre shapes, inaccessible sites spared), spider bite (loxoscelism — not UK), drug-induced (hydroxycarbamide leg ulcers, levamisole-cocaine vasculopathy), Sweet syndrome (plaques, not ulcers), Behçet's

items.t: A painful ulcer with a **purple undermined edge** that expands over days.
An ulcer getting worse after debridement or surgery (pathergy).
Systemic upset, or rapid spread despite antibiotics.

pearls.t: **Pathergy counselling:** protect the skin, and plan procedures only when the disease is quiet, with specialist input.
In the community, escalate early. Do not trial antibiotic after antibiotic.
Ask about bowel symptoms and joint pain. PG can be the first sign of IBD.
"**Graze → pustule → fast, agonising, purple-edged ulcer in someone with IBD = PG until proved otherwise — and never debride it.**"
PG is a diagnosis of exclusion: **infection first** (especially on azathioprine or a biologic), then vasculitis, vascular disease and cancer.
**Pain out of proportion** and an ulcer that **gets bigger after debridement** are the two most useful bedside clues.
Cribriform scars on the legs at a later consultation = past PG: ask about the bowel, joints and blood disorders.
Steroids and ciclosporin heal PG equally (STOP GAP): the choice is a **medicines-safety decision** — a natural place for pharmacist input.
